> **Extra session (beyond the course).** This lab is for interest and is **not part of the
> final exam**. It treats forecasting as supervised learning with a random forest (`ranger`).
> Chunks that need `ranger` skip cleanly if it is not installed: `install.packages("ranger")`.

# Packages

```{r}
library(fpp3)
has_ranger <- requireNamespace("ranger", quietly = TRUE)
has_ranger
```

# Data: Australian cafe turnover

**Turnover** is monthly sales (in millions of Australian dollars) of the industry
"Cafes, restaurants and takeaway food services". It comes from `aus_retail` (Australian
Bureau of Statistics); we sum over all states and keep 2004-2018.
We work on the log scale, as in earlier sessions.

```{r}
cafe <- aus_retail |>
  filter(Industry == "Cafes, restaurants and takeaway food services",
         year(Month) %in% 2004:2018) |>
  summarise(Turnover = sum(Turnover))
cafe |> autoplot(Turnover) + labs(title = "Australian cafe turnover", y = "$ million")
```

# From a series to a supervised-learning table

`embed(z, p + 1)` returns a matrix whose first column is $z_t$ and whose next $p$ columns
are $z_{t-1}, \dots, z_{t-p}$: one row per time point, lags as features.

```{r}
z <- log(cafe$Turnover)
E <- embed(z, 12 + 1)
colnames(E) <- c("y", paste0("lag", 1:12))
head(round(E[, 1:5], 3))
dim(E)
```

A linear regression on this table is an AR(12) estimated by least squares:

```{r}
coef(lm(y ~ ., data = as.data.frame(E)))[1:4]
```

A random forest replaces the linear combination with averages of regression trees.

# Recursive forecasting with a random forest

The function fits a forest on the lag table, then forecasts one step at a time and feeds
each forecast back in as the newest lag.

```{r}
rf_recursive <- function(z, h, p = 12, seed = 2026) {
  E <- embed(z, p + 1)
  colnames(E) <- c("y", paste0("lag", 1:p))
  set.seed(seed)
  m <- ranger::ranger(y ~ ., data = as.data.frame(E), num.trees = 500)
  hz <- z
  out <- numeric(h)
  for (i in seq_len(h)) {
    nd <- as.data.frame(t(rev(tail(hz, p))))   # newest value is lag1
    names(nd) <- paste0("lag", 1:p)
    out[i] <- predict(m, nd)$predictions
    hz <- c(hz, out[i])                         # feed the forecast back in
  }
  out
}

# (a) forest on log levels
rf_levels <- function(y, h) rf_recursive(y, h)

# (b) forest on the seasonal difference of the log, then undo the difference:
#     y_t = y_{t-12} + w_t
rf_sdiff <- function(y, h) {
  wf <- rf_recursive(diff(y, lag = 12), h)
  hy <- y
  for (i in seq_len(h)) hy <- c(hy, hy[length(hy) - 11] + wf[i])
  tail(hy, h)
}
```

# One split: train to 2016, test 2017-2018

```{r}
train <- cafe |> filter(year(Month) <= 2016)
test <- cafe |> filter(year(Month) >= 2017)
h <- nrow(test)

fc_stat <- train |>
  model(snaive = SNAIVE(log(Turnover)),
        ets = ETS(log(Turnover)),
        arima = ARIMA(log(Turnover))) |>
  forecast(h = h)
acc <- accuracy(fc_stat, cafe) |> select(.model, RMSE)
acc
```

```{r, eval = has_ranger}
ly <- log(train$Turnover)
fc_ml <- tibble(Month = test$Month,
                rf_levels = exp(rf_levels(ly, h)),
                rf_sdiff = exp(rf_sdiff(ly, h)))
rmse <- function(f) sqrt(mean((test$Turnover - f)^2))
acc_all <- bind_rows(acc, tibble(.model = c("rf_levels", "rf_sdiff"),
                                 RMSE = c(rmse(fc_ml$rf_levels), rmse(fc_ml$rf_sdiff))))
acc_all |> arrange(RMSE)
```

# Trees cannot extrapolate

A tree predicts an average of training targets, so the forest on levels can never go above
the largest value it has seen.

```{r, eval = has_ranger}
c(train_max = max(train$Turnover),
  rf_levels_max = max(fc_ml$rf_levels),
  test_max = max(test$Turnover))

fc_ml |>
  pivot_longer(-Month, names_to = "model", values_to = "Turnover") |>
  ggplot(aes(Month, Turnover, colour = model)) +
  geom_line(data = cafe |> filter(year(Month) >= 2012) |> as_tibble(),
            aes(Month, Turnover), colour = "black", inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = max(train$Turnover), linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Random forest forecasts, 2017-2018",
       subtitle = "Dashed line: largest value in the training data", y = "$ million")
```

Modelling the seasonal difference turns an extrapolation problem (a growing level) into
an interpolation problem (changes that stay in a familiar range). This is the same idea as
$d$ and $D$ in ARIMA.

# Rolling origins: is the forest really better?

One hold-out is one draw. Repeat the comparison for five forecast origins
(train up to 2012, ..., 2016; test the next 2 years each time).

```{r, eval = has_ranger}
run_origin <- function(end_year) {
  tr <- cafe |> filter(year(Month) <= end_year)
  te <- cafe |> filter(year(Month) %in% (end_year + 1):(end_year + 2))
  h <- nrow(te)
  st <- tr |>
    model(snaive = SNAIVE(log(Turnover)), ets = ETS(log(Turnover)),
          arima = ARIMA(log(Turnover))) |>
    forecast(h = h) |>
    accuracy(cafe) |>
    select(.model, RMSE)
  ly <- log(tr$Turnover)
  r <- function(f) sqrt(mean((te$Turnover - f)^2))
  bind_rows(st, tibble(.model = c("rf_levels", "rf_sdiff"),
                       RMSE = c(r(exp(rf_levels(ly, h))), r(exp(rf_sdiff(ly, h)))))) |>
    mutate(origin = end_year)
}
rolling <- bind_rows(lapply(2012:2016, run_origin))

rolling |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = origin, values_from = RMSE) |>
  mutate(mean = rowMeans(across(-.model))) |>
  arrange(mean) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), round))
```

```{r, eval = has_ranger}
rolling |>
  group_by(origin) |>
  slice_min(RMSE, n = 1) |>
  select(origin, winner = .model, RMSE)
```

**Read the table.** Which model wins the 2016 origin (the single split above)? Which model
has the lowest *mean* RMSE? How many origins does `rf_sdiff` win?

# Your turn

1. **Lags.** Refit `rf_sdiff` with `p = 24` lags instead of 12. Does the mean rolling-origin
   RMSE improve?
2. **Another learner.** Replace the forest with a linear model on the same lag table
   (`lm(y ~ ., ...)`). How does this "AR(12) on seasonal differences" compare with
   `rf_sdiff` and with `ARIMA()`?
3. **Neural network.** `fable` has a neural network autoregression (FPP3 Section 12.4):
   add `nnar = NNETAR(log(Turnover))` to the `model()` call of the single split (it can take
   a minute; use `set.seed()` first). Where does it rank? Does it extrapolate the trend?
4. **Leakage.** Suppose you add a feature "mean of $y$ over the 12 months *centred* on $t$".
   Why would this give an excellent test RMSE and useless real forecasts?
